title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
one_line_takeaway: Most of our judgements come from a fast, intuitive System 1 whose shortcuts produce predictable errors, and knowing where those errors lie is the best defence against them.
synopsis:
Daniel Kahneman, a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in economics, distils decades of research — much of it with his late collaborator Amos Tversky — into a portrait of how the mind makes judgements and choices. He describes two modes of thinking as characters: System 1, which is fast, automatic and intuitive, and System 2, which is slow, effortful and deliberate. System 2 believes it is in charge, but it is lazy and mostly endorses what System 1 proposes.

The first half of the book catalogues the heuristics System 1 relies on and the biases they produce: jumping to conclusions from whatever information is at hand ('what you see is all there is'), substituting an easier question for a hard one, anchoring on irrelevant numbers, judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind, and ignoring base rates in favour of a representative story. Kahneman then turns to overconfidence: the illusion that we understand the past, the illusion of validity that lets experts trust unreliable judgements, the superiority of simple formulas over expert intuition in noisy domains, and the planning fallacy.

The later parts challenge the rational agent of economics. Prospect theory, the work that earned the Nobel, shows that people evaluate outcomes as gains and losses from a reference point, feel losses about twice as strongly as gains, and weigh probabilities non-linearly — which explains framing effects, the endowment effect and the fourfold pattern of risk attitudes. The book closes with two selves: the experiencing self that lives through moments and the remembering self that keeps score and makes decisions, whose memories follow the peak-end rule and neglect duration.

ideas.title: Two systems
ideas.summary: Thinking runs on two modes: System 1 operates automatically and quickly with no sense of voluntary control, while System 2 allocates attention to effortful mental activity. System 2 is lazy, so System 1's quick answers usually go unchecked.
ideas.evidence: The bat-and-ball problem: a bat and ball cost $1.10 and the bat costs $1 more than the ball; most people, including many students at elite universities, answer that the ball costs 10 cents instead of 5.

ideas.title: What you see is all there is
ideas.summary: System 1 builds the most coherent story it can from the information available and doesn't account for what is missing, so confidence reflects the coherence of a story, not the quality or quantity of evidence behind it.
ideas.evidence: Solomon Asch's descriptions of Alan (intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, envious) and Ben (the same traits in reverse order): the order changes the impression, an instance of the halo effect.

ideas.title: Substitution and anchoring
ideas.summary: Faced with a hard question, System 1 often answers an easier related one without noticing. Anchoring is a related failure: an arbitrary number considered before an estimate pulls the estimate toward it.
ideas.evidence: A wheel of fortune rigged to stop at 10 or 65 shifted people's estimates of the percentage of African nations in the UN, to averages of 25% and 45% respectively.

ideas.title: Availability
ideas.summary: People judge how frequent or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid, recent or heavily reported events seem more common than they are.
ideas.evidence: In a study by Norbert Schwarz, people asked to list twelve instances of their own assertive behaviour rated themselves as less assertive than those asked to list six, because the later instances were hard to recall.

ideas.title: Representativeness and base rates
ideas.summary: Judging probability by how well something matches a stereotype leads people to ignore base rates and even the rules of logic.
ideas.evidence: The Linda problem: most people judge 'Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement' more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller', a conjunction fallacy. Tom W's personality sketch led people to ignore how few graduate students study his stereotyped field.

ideas.title: Regression to the mean
ideas.summary: Extreme performances tend to be followed by more ordinary ones by chance alone, but the mind invents causal stories to explain the change.
ideas.evidence: Israeli Air Force flight instructors believed praise made cadets worse and criticism made them better; Kahneman showed they were seeing regression to the mean after unusually good and bad manoeuvres.

ideas.title: The illusions of understanding and validity
ideas.summary: Hindsight and the narrative fallacy make the past look more predictable than it was, and people keep trusting their judgements even when evidence shows those judgements have little predictive value.
ideas.evidence: Kahneman's own army evaluations of officer candidates in a leaderless group exercise felt compelling but barely predicted later performance; the year-to-year performance of the financial advisers at an investment firm showed essentially zero correlation, like a game of chance.

ideas.title: Formulas beat intuition, and when intuition can be trusted
ideas.summary: In uncertain, noisy environments simple statistical rules outperform expert judgement. Expert intuition is reliable only in a regular environment where the expert has had long practice with quick feedback.
ideas.evidence: Paul Meehl's review of clinical versus statistical prediction; the Apgar score for newborns; Kahneman's joint work with Gary Klein, a defender of expert intuition, on the conditions under which it is skilled.

ideas.title: The planning fallacy and the outside view
ideas.summary: Plans and forecasts are unrealistically close to best-case scenarios because people take the inside view of their own case. Consulting the base rate of similar projects — the outside view — corrects it.
ideas.evidence: Kahneman's team writing a decision-making curriculum estimated about two years to finish; their own curriculum expert admitted similar teams took seven to ten years and about 40% never finished. The project took eight years.

ideas.title: Prospect theory and loss aversion
ideas.summary: People evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, not as states of wealth, with diminishing sensitivity in both directions. Losses loom larger than equivalent gains, roughly twice as large.
ideas.evidence: 'Bernoulli's error': expected utility theory ignored reference points. Most people refuse a coin toss that loses $100 or wins $150.

ideas.title: The fourfold pattern, the endowment effect and framing
ideas.summary: Because people overweight small probabilities and underweight near-certainties, they are risk-averse for likely gains and unlikely losses but risk-seeking for likely losses and unlikely gains. Owning something raises its value to us, and logically equivalent descriptions produce different choices.
ideas.evidence: The Asian disease problem: people prefer the certain option when outcomes are framed as lives saved and the gamble when the same outcomes are framed as lives lost. Lotteries and insurance both fit the fourfold pattern.

ideas.title: The experiencing self and the remembering self
ideas.summary: The remembering self keeps score and makes decisions, but it evaluates experiences by their peak and their end and neglects their duration, so we choose for memories rather than for experience.
ideas.evidence: In the cold-hand experiment most people chose to repeat a longer episode of immersion in cold water that ended slightly less painfully; colonoscopy patients' memories tracked the worst moment and the final moments of the procedure.

key_claims_for_review.answer: System 1 is fast, automatic and effortless and runs constantly; System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful. System 2 is lazy and mostly endorses System 1's suggestions.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What does 'what you see is all there is' (WYSIATI) mean?
key_claims_for_review.answer: System 1 builds a coherent story from the information at hand and ignores what's missing, so confidence tracks the coherence of the story rather than the quality of the evidence.
An estimate is pulled toward a number considered beforehand, even an obviously random one, like the number a rigged wheel of fortune stopped on.
Judging how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What does the Linda problem show?
key_claims_for_review.answer: People judge a specific, representative conjunction ('bank teller and feminist') more probable than one of its parts — the conjunction fallacy, produced by judging by representativeness rather than probability.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: How did Kahneman explain the flight instructors' belief that criticism works better than praise?
key_claims_for_review.answer: Regression to the mean: an unusually good performance tends to be followed by a worse one and an unusually bad one by a better one, whatever the instructor says.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: When can expert intuition be trusted?
key_claims_for_review.answer: Only in an environment regular enough to be predictable, where the expert has had prolonged practice with rapid, clear feedback.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What is the planning fallacy, and what corrects it?
key_claims_for_review.answer: Forecasts that sit close to best-case scenarios because people take the inside view of their own project. The outside view — the base rate of similar projects — corrects it.
Losses loom larger than gains of the same size, roughly twice as large, so people refuse many favourable gambles.
Expected utility theory evaluated outcomes as states of wealth; it missed that people evaluate them as gains and losses from a reference point.
People are risk-averse for high-probability gains and low-probability losses (insurance), and risk-seeking for high-probability losses and low-probability gains (lotteries).
The remembering self rates an experience by its most intense moment and how it ended, neglecting how long it lasted.
